Would remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) deference to prior USCIS approvals, so a re-filed EOS/OPT-type request would be decided on the record afresh - relevant to students who must file again after an approval. **Not in force** (comments closed Nov. 13, 2026).
8. **FR Doc. 2026-20955**, final rule (DHS), **Oct. 14, 2026**, 91 FR 65306. Ends automatic extensions of expiring EADs for renewal applications filed on or after **Oct. 30, 2025** (new 8 CFR 274a.13(e)), so EAD renewals can lapse; it does not disturb the separate **180-day** STEM OPT auto-extension in 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv). **In force** (effective Oct. 14, 2026).","basis":"FR Docs 2026-16231 (91 FR 51360), 2026-17324 (91 FR 54817; correction 91 FR 57516), 2026-18631 (91 FR 57807), 2026-19554 (91 FR 60497), 2026-19555 (91 FR 60501), 2026-20660 (91 FR 64566), 2026-20941 (91 FR 65119), 2026-20955 (91 FR 65306, 65307, 65309-65310); 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) as preserved by FR Doc. 2026-14439, 91 FR 45101.","uncertainty":"None of the proposed rules has a predictable final form or date; the Proclamation's payment mechanics (who verifies, how) are left to DHS/State implementation, which is not in the Federal Register as of Nov. 14, 2026."},"Q11":{"answer":"**What the final rule says about cost.** The rule does not set a dollar fee for Form I-539. It says (i) 'USCIS is a fee-funded agency and established fees for the EOS applications to support the workload associated with adjudication of cases,' and conducts biennial fee studies (91 FR 45083-45084); (ii) every F-1 applicant must remit 'the appropriate fee' and any required biometrics (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)); and (iii) if a dependent files a separate I-539 a separate fee is required, but if the dependent is included via Form I-539A on the principal's I-539 'only one fee will be required' (91 FR 45110; 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2), 214.2(f)(7)(iv)). The only dollar figures in the document are **commenter statements** - a **$420** filing fee (91 FR 45055) and **$555 per application including biometrics** (91 FR 45065) - and DHS's regulatory-impact assumption of an average **$490** in legal-support cost for the 24.5% of applicants expected to need help, drawn from the Form I-539 supporting statement (91 FR 45083).

**What it says about how long USCIS takes.** DHS states that '80 percent of Form I-539 adjudications for F, M, and J aliens are completed in three months' (91 FR 45084 & n.277, citing USCIS Case Processing Times) - while acknowledging backlogs and stating that it 'cannot guarantee processing times' (91 FR 45025; see also 91 FR 45009). The rule also gives a bridging figure: a timely EOS filing keeps the student in authorized stay until USCIS decides (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)), and extends on-campus/CPT/severe-economic-hardship employment for up to **240 days** from the I-94 end date (same provision; 91 FR 45106-45107).

**Handout sentences an adviser could accurately use:**
1. 'A student who needs more time files Form I-539 with USCIS and pays USCIS's I-539 filing fee (plus biometrics if required; the amount is set by USCIS's fee schedule, not by the 2026 student rule), and a dependent can be included on the same application with one fee.'
2. 'DHS says about 80 percent of Form I-539 applications filed by F, M and J nonimmigrants are decided within three months, but DHS does not guarantee processing times; if the application is timely filed, the student may remain while it is pending, and on-campus or CPT work can continue for up to 240 days after the I-94 date.'","basis":"FR Doc. 2026-14439, 91 FR 45083, 45084 & n.277 (fee-funded agency; 80%/three months), 45055 and 45065 (commenter fee figures of $420 and $555), 45083 (n.275 $490 legal-support assumption), 45025 and 45009 (no guarantee of processing times), 45106-45107 (240-day employment continuation), 45110 (dependent fees; I-539A); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(iii)(A), (f)(7)(iv); 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2).","uncertainty":"The rule contains no authoritative fee amount and no service-level commitment; the $420/$555 figures are commenter statements and DHS's 'three months' statement is a historical processing statistic, not a guarantee. Any handout figure should be tied to USCIS's current fee schedule and case-processing-time page rather than to the rule."},"Q12":{"answer":"(a) **Yes - a I-539 received during the 60 days after her program end date is timely, as long as it is received by July 14, 2027.** Basis: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) gives her an authorized period of stay running to the program end date plus 60 days (May 15, 2027 + 60 = July 14, 2027; see 91 FR 45017 and 45099), and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) makes an EOS application timely if 'the receipt date ... is on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires,' including the departure period. 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) also directs a transition-group student who wants to start a new program to file the EOS under 214.1(c)(2). One caveat: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) speaks of the '30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v),' and the transition provision uses 60 days; the better reading (and DHS's own description at 91 FR 45099) is that her authorized period includes the 60 days, so receipt through July 14, 2027 is timely.

(b) **No - filing during that 60-day window does not carry the automatic extension of on-campus or CPT employment.** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) provides the employment auto-extension (up to 240 days) only where the EOS is timely filed before the authorized employment period ends, and it expressly denies the benefit to a student who files 'during the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)' - who 'does not receive an automatic extension of authorized employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship, and must wait for approval' (91 FR 45111 n.327). The same logic applies to the transition group's 60-day departure period, and in any event her on-campus employment authorization is tied to the end of her authorized employment period (30 days before the I-94 admit-until date under (f)(5)(viii)'s I-9 rule) and to continued enrollment.

**Recommendation for the adviser:** treat two deadlines separately. (1) **Status:** an I-539 received by **July 14, 2027** is timely, so a filing in the 60 days will not by itself put her out of status. (2) **Work:** if she has on-campus or CPT employment she wants to continue without interruption, the I-539 should be received **before May 15, 2027** (the program end date), not merely before July 14, 2027; a filing in the 60 days means no work until USCIS approves. If she has no employment to preserve, filing within the 60 days is acceptable, but filing earlier reduces risk given the (f)(5)(v)/(m)(1) cross-reference ambiguity. Advise documenting the DSO-endorsed new I-20, funds, and the change of program ((f)(7)(ii)-(iii)(A)).","basis":"8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) and (m)(1)(i), 91 FR 45123-45124; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v), (f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(ii)-(iii)(B), 91 FR 45124-45126; preamble 91 FR 45017 (transition 30/60 days), 45099 (program end date plus 60 days), 45106-45107 (240-day employment; stop after 240 days), 45111 & n.327 (no employment extension if filed in the departure period).","uncertainty":"The rule never says in terms whether the 60-day transition period counts as part of the 'authorized period of stay' for the (f)(7)(iii)(B) timeliness test; (f)(7)(iii)(B)'s express cross-reference is to the 30-day period in (f)(5)(v). A stricter USCIS reading would make a filing after May 15, 2027 untimely, which is why filing before the program end date is the safer course."},"Q13":{"answer":"(a) **June 13, 2027.** Because she departs and is readmitted, her D/S transition period is replaced by a fixed period of admission: 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) (admission for 'a maximum period of 4 years or the length of program as specified on Form I-20, whichever is shorter, plus additional 30 day periods for arrival and departure') and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(v) (the 30-day departure period is reflected on the I-94). Arithmetic: program end date May 14, 2027 + 30 days = **June 13, 2027** (the 4-year alternative is longer and therefore not the limit). Compare 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1): had she not traveled, her D/S authorization would have run to May 14, 2027 + 60 days = July 13, 2027 - so the January trip shortened her filing-free period by 30 days (see 91 FR 45099: upon travel the admission period becomes the I-20 program end date 'plus the currently permitted additional period of 60 days for F nonimmigrants and 30 days for J nonimmigrants' *before* travel, but new admissions carry only 30 days).

(b) **Yes - she must file a Form I-539, and USCIS must receive it on or before June 13, 2027.** Although 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) normally exempts a recommended post-completion OPT applicant who files an I-765 on or before March 18, 2027 from filing an I-539, **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii) removes that exemption for a student who 'departs the United States before filing the application for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT, and is admitted to the United States with a fixed period of admission'** - that student 'is required to file both' the I-765 and the I-539. Sofia left on Dec. 19, 2026 and was readmitted Jan. 9, 2027, *before* she filed the I-765 (Feb. 22, 2027), so (m)(1)(ii) applies. Timeline: I-539 receipt deadline = expiration of her authorized period, **June 13, 2027** (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) also requires the EOS because she is outside (m)(1)(i)). Practical note: if the I-539 is received during the 30-day period (May 14-June 13, 2027), she may keep studying but may not begin OPT until the EOS is approved (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B); 91 FR 45111), so she should file earlier if she wants a seamless OPT start on June 10, 2027.

(c) **July 9, 2028.** OPT EAD ends June 9, 2028; because she is on the EOS track, the extension includes the additional 30-day departure period: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) ('the student extension will include the additional 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)') and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi). June 9, 2028 + 30 days = July 9, 2028. (Had she never traveled and therefore qualified under (m)(1)(i), the end date would be EAD plus 60 days = Aug. 8, 2028.)

(d) **No I-539 is needed, and she may be readmitted for the OPT period plus 30 days - carrying the I-765 receipt notice and the OPT-endorsed I-20.** On these facts she filed the I-765 on Feb. 22, 2027 - before her period of admission expired and on or before March 18, 2027 - so 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) exempts her from the I-539, and the later trip during the 30-day departure period does not change that ((m)(1)(ii) is triggered only by departing *before* filing the OPT application). On re-entry, 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii) allows admission 'until the end date of the approved employment authorization for post-completion OPT ... or if the Application for Employment Authorization ... is still pending with USCIS, as evidenced by a notice issued by USCIS indicating receipt of such application, until the Designated School Official's recommended employment end date for post-completion OPT ..., plus a 30-day period.' Here that is June 9, 2028 + 30 days = **July 9, 2028**. **Carry:** the Form I-797C receipt notice for the I-765 and the DSO-endorsed I-20 showing the OPT recommendation (8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(iii); 214.1(a)(4)(iii); 91 FR 45098-45100), plus the EAD if it has been issued by the time she travels, and a valid passport/visa.","basis":"8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A), (a)(4)(iii), (c)(8)(iii), (m)(1)(i)-(ii), as added by FR Doc. 2026-14439, 91 FR 45122-45124; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(v), (f)(7)(iii)(B), (f)(7)(vi), (f)(10)(ii)(D), 91 FR 45124-45127; preamble 91 FR 45098-45099 (readmission scenarios and what to carry), 45099 (transition period upon travel), 45101 (I-539/I-765 for travelers before filing), 45111 (no employment if EOS filed in the 30-day period).","uncertainty":"Admission under 214.1(a)(4)(iii) is discretionary ('may be admitted'), and the rule does not say whether CBP will admit to the DSO-recommended end date if the I-765 is approved but the EAD has not yet been delivered; ICE guidance cited in the rule suggests traveling with the EAD in hand where possible (91 FR 45100 n.303)."},"Q14":{"answer":"(a) **Document: 'Optional Practical Training Fees,' FR Doc. 2026-20660, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)**, a **proposed rule (NPRM)** issued by **DHS/U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)**, Docket **DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100**, RIN **1653-AB01**, affecting 8 CFR part 214 (proposed new 8 CFR 214.13(i) and conforming changes to 214.2(f)(11)). **Status: proposed only; not in force.** Deadlines it sets: comments must be received **on or before Nov. 9, 2026**; comments on the information collection must be received **by Dec. 7, 2026**. It proposes **$70,000 for initial OPT** and **$30,000 for any subsequent OPT**, payable by the SEVP-certified school.

(b) **On the literal text, $70,000 would apply to Daniel's STEM OPT extension - not $30,000.** Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2) imposes the $30,000 only 'if the alien has previously participated in OPT **and paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000**.' Daniel has participated in OPT but never paid $70,000 (his post-completion OPT was approved before any fee existed), so the $30,000 condition is not satisfied. Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3) (transition) then supplies the operative rule for his case: schools 'must pay the fee of $70,000 for each alien who receives a DSO recommendation for OPT that is dated on or after [60 days after publication of the final rule]'; the $30,000 applies only to 'subsequent DSO recommendations ... for which the $70,000 OPT fee has been paid.' DHS's discussion in section V.A says the $30,000 applies to 'any type of OPT ... after having completed their initial OPT' for a student 'who ... has previously paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000' (91 FR 64577), and its reliance discussion says only that a student whose OPT predates the rule must pay if he 'submits a subsequent request for OPT on or after the effective date' (91 FR 64578-64579) - without saying which amount. The **$30,000 reading** is supportable only if one treats the payment condition in (i)(2) as surplusage and keys 'subsequent' solely to prior participation; DHS's cost narrative appears to assume students pay $70,000 plus $30,000 across initial and STEM OPT (91 FR 64583).

(c) **Who pays, when, consequences, refunds.** The **SEVP-certified educational institution** pays - not the student, and not tied to any employer (91 FR 64577: the fee 'would not be tied to a specific employer'). **When:** before the DSO enters the OPT recommendation in SEVIS ('This payment must be made prior to the DSO recommending a student for OPT,' proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2); the DSO must confirm payment before updating SEVIS, 91 FR 64577). **If not paid:** the DSO may not enter the recommendation; USCIS 'would not grant employment authorization to any student' where the school failed to pay (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii); 91 FR 64577), and the student's I-765 cannot proceed. **Refundable?** Only at SEVP's discretion, case-by-case: a school may request a refund if the student has not yet been issued the EAD; 'this fee will not be refunded under any circumstances once the F-1 student has been granted the employment authorization document'; the DSO must first remove the OPT recommendation in SEVIS; determinations are final and not appealable (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2); 91 FR 64577).

(d) **When it would apply.** The proposed rule would take effect **60 days after publication of the final rule** (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3); 91 FR 64577), and the fee applies to students who 'receive[] a DSO recommendation for OPT that is dated on or after' that date. The trigger is the **date of the DSO's recommendation**, not the date the I-765 is filed: DHS says institutions need not pay for a student 'currently engaging in previously approved OPT, has been approved for OPT prior to the effective date ..., or has received a DSO recommendation for OPT prior to the effective date' (91 FR 64578-64579). So **yes** - if Daniel's DSO dated the STEM OPT recommendation **before** the final rule's effective date, his extension would fall outside the fee; a recommendation dated April 2027 would be inside it only if the final rule were published and took effect before April 2027, which cannot be known yet (as of Nov. 14, 2026 the NPRM is not final). The documents do not state the earliest date on which a DSO may issue a STEM OPT recommendation (that timing lives in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11), which this NPRM does not amend), so the feasible window for an early recommendation cannot be fixed from these documents.

(e) **Under the rules in force today, Daniel must file two things: Form I-765 for the STEM OPT extension and Form I-539 for an extension of stay.** Because he is a D/S transition student and will not file the I-765 on or before **March 18, 2027** (he plans April 12, 2027), the I-539 exemption in 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) is unavailable; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) requires a student recommended for OPT to obtain the EAD 'and either apply for an extension of stay with USCIS or seek admission through CBP after travel abroad,' and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7) and 214.1(m)(1) supply the EOS mechanism (with the DSO-endorsed I-20). His I-539 must be received before his authorized period expires - under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) that is the later of his EAD end date (June 30, 2027) or program end date, plus 60 days, i.e., about Aug. 29, 2027; his April 12, 2027 filing is timely. **Work authorization while pending:** his post-completion OPT EAD is automatically extended for up to **180 days** while the STEM OPT I-765 is pending under 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) - a provision the final rule left intact and expressly acknowledged (8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii); 91 FR 45101: STEM OPT filers 'remain eligible for the 180-day extension of their post-completion OPT EAD while their application for STEM OPT is pending'). **If approved:** the STEM OPT period runs 24 months from July 1, 2027 through **June 30, 2029**, and with the EOS his stay includes the 30-day departure period, i.e., to **July 30, 2029** (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi); (f)(10)(ii)(D); (f)(5)(v)).","basis":"FR Doc. 2026-20660, 91 FR 64566, 64577, 64578-64579, 64581, 64583, 64599-64600 (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(3), 214.2(f)(11)(ii)-(iii)), and FR metadata (comments Nov. 9, 2026; PRA comments Dec. 7, 2026); 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i), 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B), (f)(7)(vi), (f)(10)(ii)(D), 214.1(a)(4)(iii) (FR Doc. 2026-14439, 91 FR 45123-45127); 91 FR 45101 (180-day STEM OPT extension); 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv); FR Doc. 2026-20955, 91 FR 65306 (does not amend 274a.12(b)(6)(iv)).","uncertainty":"The proposed text is internally inconsistent for students in Daniel's position (prior OPT participation but no prior $70,000 payment), and DHS may clarify or change it in a final rule. Whether the 180-day STEM OPT auto-extension is available when the student also has a pending EOS is not addressed in these documents; the rule treats the EAD extension and the stay extension as separate mechanisms. All amounts are proposals, not current law."},"Q15":{"answer":"**1. Incorrect (as stated).** The deadline is not the I-20 program end date. 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) requires USCIS to receive the application 'on or before the expiration of the authorized period of stay, including the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v),' and expressly displaces the usual late-filing tolerance ('Notwithstanding Sec. 214.1(c)(4)'). For a fixed-period admission the I-94 runs to the program end date plus 30 days (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(v); 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)); for a transition-group student the period runs to program end plus 60 days (214.1(m)(1)). *Reworded:* 'USCIS must receive the extension application on or before the date printed on the student's I-94 (generally the program end date plus 30 days; for students still on the D/S transition, generally the program end date plus 60 days). Filing in that trailing period is timely, but the student may not work (and may not start CPT/OPT) while the application is pending.'

**2. Incorrect.** The 4-year maximum is not counted from the day of entry. DHS states: 'The calculation of the 4-year maximum period of admission will not begin from the date of admission during that 30-day arrival window, but from the program start date,' and the 30-day arrival and departure periods 'do not count towards the maximum' (91 FR 45098-45099; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)). For D/S transition students the 4 years runs from **Sept. 15, 2026** (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)). *Reworded:* 'The four-year cap is measured from the program start date (not the date of entry), the 30 days before the start date and 30 days after the end date do not count, and for students who were in D/S on Sept. 15, 2026 the four-year clock runs from that date.'

**3. Correct.** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii): a student whose I-94 has expired but who timely filed an EOS 'will be considered to be in a period of authorized stay ... until USCIS issues a decision,' while on-campus/CPT/severe-economic-hardship employment is auto-extended only 'up to 240 days beginning from the end date of his or her period of admission as indicated on' the I-94. DHS says so directly: 'If the EOS application is still pending after 240 days have passed, the F-1 student will no longer be authorized for employment and will need to stop engaging in on-campus employment' (91 FR 45106-45107). *Suggested tightening:* add that the 240 days run from the I-94 date and that study may continue because the stay authorization is not capped at 240 days.

**4. Incorrect.** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A) limits an English-language-training student to 'a maximum of admission period of 24 months, plus an additional 30-day period of stay,' with no medical exception. DHS expressly rejected the point: 'Students who encounter extenuating circumstances such as illness, disability, or other emergencies during their studies, will still be limited to the 24-month admission period' (91 FR 45039). *Reworded:* 'The 24-month limit on English-language study applies even if the student becomes ill or has another emergency; the student may depart and re-enter but will not receive additional admission time for time spent abroad.'

**5. Incorrect.** DHS addressed this head-on: 'The commenters are mistaken when they think that accredited programs will need to be shortened to fit the 4-year admission period. That is untrue. If the program has been accredited as a 5-year program, the I-20 ... will state the full program length. The student will need to apply for an EOS with USCIS prior to the expiration of his or her currently authorized period of stay using the same I-20 ... and may continue to study while the application is pending' (91 FR 45039). *Reworded:* 'A five-year accredited program is not shortened and does not require two I-20s; the I-20 shows the full length, the student is admitted for the four-year maximum, and the student files an extension of stay for the balance, using the same I-20.'

**6. Partly correct - and the qualification matters.** Yes, a student readmitted on an I-20 with a later program end date can receive a new fixed period from CBP: 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B) (admission for the period specified in 214.2(f)(5), i.e., program length not to exceed 4 years, plus 30 days), and DHS's readmission scenarios at 91 FR 45098 confirm that aliens who departed without an approved EOS 'may be admitted for the length of time as indicated by the program end date noted in their Form I-20 ... not to exceed 4 years, plus a period of 30 days.' **But:** (i) admission is discretionary ('may'), not an entitlement; (ii) if an EOS was pending, it 'may be deemed abandoned' when the alien seeks admission with an I-20 bearing a later program end date, and 'the AUD provided by CBP on the alien's I-94 would govern' (8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii); 91 FR 45098, 45100); and (iii) the new period is still capped at 4 years or program length, so a program that extends beyond that cap still requires an EOS. *Reworded:* 'If a student travels and is readmitted on an I-20 with a later program end date, CBP may admit the student for a new fixed period (program length, up to 4 years, plus 30 days), which replaces any pending extension request; the student does not need a USCIS extension for the time covered by that new I-94, but admission is discretionary and the four-year cap still applies.'

**7. Incorrect on both the trigger and the date.** 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i), as adopted, exempts a recommended post-completion OPT applicant who files the I-765 'before his or her period of admission expires, including the 60 day departure period, ... on or before **March 18, 2027**' (and, for STEM OPT, before the current OPT EAD expires) - a fixed date, not 'six months.' Six months from the Sept. 15, 2026 effective date would be **March 15, 2027**, which is *not* the date in the rule. **Where text and preamble diverge:** the preamble of the final rule loosely describes the exemption as filing 'within six months of the rule's effective date' (91 FR 45034), tracking the NPRM's formulation (90 FR 42084); the operative text fixes March 18, 2027 (91 FR 45123). **The regulatory text controls** - it is the operative rule, was adopted later in the rulemaking, and is the more specific and more generous date - so advisers should use **March 18, 2027**. Also note 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii) reserves DHS discretion to extend the exemption in six-month increments by Federal Register notice. *Reworded:* 'A student recommended for post-completion OPT (or STEM OPT) who files Form I-765 on or before March 18, 2027, and before the student's period of admission expires, does not need to file Form I-539 for that OPT period; DHS may extend the March 18, 2027 date by Federal Register notice.'","basis":"Items 1-3: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(v), (f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(iii)(B); 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1); 91 FR 45098-45099, 45106-45107, 45111. Item 4: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A); 91 FR 45039. Item 5: 91 FR 45039. Item 6: 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B), (c)(8)(ii); 91 FR 45098, 45100. Item 7: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) and (iii), 91 FR 45123; preamble 91 FR 45034; NPRM 90 FR 42084.","uncertainty":"For item 7, the preamble/text conflict is genuine (six months vs. March 18, 2027), and the rule does not explain the three-day difference; for item 6, the rule does not state how the four-year cap is applied on a mid-program readmission (the 'count from the program start date' sentence at 91 FR 45099 is framed for initial admissions)."},"Q16":{"answer":"(a) **September 22, 2031.** 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) (admission for a maximum of 4 years or the program length on the I-20, whichever is shorter, plus 30-day arrival and departure periods) and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i). Arithmetic: her program is longer than 4 years, so the 4-year cap controls; per DHS, the 4 years run from the **program start date**, not from the Aug. 2, 2027 entry (91 FR 45098-45099). Aug. 23, 2027 + 4 years = **Aug. 23, 2031**; add the 30-day departure period = **Sept. 22, 2031** (Aug. 24-31 = 8 days; Sept. 22 = 30). The 21 days of early arrival (Aug. 2-22) do not shorten the period.

(b) **She must file Form I-539 for an extension of stay before Sept. 22, 2031**, with a DSO-endorsed I-20 showing the new (or same) program end date, evidence of funds, biometrics if required, and the fee - 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)-(iii) and 214.1(c)(2). **Ground:** she must show she 'is unable to complete his or her program by the end of his or her authorized period of admission' and has (1) a currently issued I-20 indicating additional time, or (2) documentation of a qualifying reason - a compelling academic reason (e.g., change of major or research topic, unexpected research problems such as an unexpected change in faculty advisor, research funding delays), a documented compelling medical reason, or circumstances beyond her control (natural disaster, national health crisis, institutional closure) (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)). **How early:** there is no regulatory earliest date - DHS says in a footnote that 'there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date ahead of expiration,' while encouraging filing within the six months before expiration (91 FR 45107 & n.328; 91 FR 45110 & n.338). **If granted in full:** an extension for the time needed to complete the program, not to exceed 4 years, plus the 30-day departure period - i.e., program end **May 14, 2033 + 30 days = June 13, 2033** (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi); (f)(5)(v)).

(c) **No - it does not jeopardize the PhD.** Completing a master's en route to a doctorate is progression to a **higher** educational level, which the rule treats as maintaining F-1 status (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B)). The same-or-lower-level prohibition in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) does not apply because the PhD is at a higher level than the master's. The graduate-level bar on changing educational objectives/transferring ((f)(5)(ii)(A)) is also not implicated, because she is not changing objectives or schools - the master's is an intermediate award within the same doctoral program of study. (Her EOS application should still be supported by the DSO-endorsed I-20 showing the full program end date, which is what (f)(7)(i)(C)(1) contemplates.)

(d) **She could be admitted to June 13, 2033, and would not need the extension in (b) - but the answer is only moderately certain.** 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) (via 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B)'s reference to the period in 214.2(f)(5)) allows admission 'for the length of time as indicated by the program end date noted in [the] Form I-20 ... not to exceed 4 years, plus a period of 30 days to prepare for departure' (91 FR 45098). Because her I-20 program end date (May 14, 2033) is less than four years from an August 2030 admission, that period is the program length: May 14, 2033 + 30 = **June 13, 2033**, and no EOS would be needed for the remaining time. **Certainty flagged:** the rule says CBP 'may' admit (discretion); the rule does not expressly address how the 4-year cap is computed for a mid-program readmission (DHS's 'count from the program start date' statement at 91 FR 45099 is framed for initial admissions in the 30-day arrival window, and applied literally to a 2030 readmission would produce a nonsensical result); and no EOS is pending in this scenario, so 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii) abandonment is not in play. An adviser should treat the June 13, 2033 admission as likely but not guaranteed, and should not let the (b) extension be abandoned without confirming the new I-94.

(e) **Until September 22, 2031** - her husband may not stay beyond Lin's authorized period, even if his I-94 shows a later date: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E) ('[t]he authorized period of stay for F-2 dependents may not exceed the authorized period of stay of the principal F-1 student') and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi). (A later F-2 admit-until date would be an error; the principal's date controls.) **Coverage when Lin applies:** he must either be included in her I-539 or file his own extension application, with the qualifying relationship shown and the appropriate fee (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv)); his extension cannot exceed hers. **Fee:** a dependent included on the principal's Form I-539 via Form I-539A requires only one fee; a dependent who files a separate Form I-539 must pay a separate filing fee (91 FR 45110; 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2)).","basis":"8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)-(B), 214.1(c)(2), 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(i)(E), (f)(5)(v), (f)(7)(i)(C), (f)(7)(iv), (f)(7)(vi), as added by FR Doc. 2026-14439, 91 FR 45122-45127; preamble 91 FR 45098-45099 (4-year calculation from program start date; readmission with a valid I-20 for program length plus 30 days), 45107 & n.328 and 45110 & n.338 (no earliest filing date; DHS encourages filing within six months), 45110 (F-2 included vs. separate filing and fees).","uncertainty":"The 4-year computation for a mid-program readmission is not spelled out, and CBP admission is discretionary; the rule also does not address what happens if a dependent's I-94 is erroneously issued beyond the principal's authorized stay (the regulation makes the principal's date controlling, but correction through CBP/USCIS is not described in the Federal Register)."}}

Q1.answer:
(a) **FR Doc. 2026-14439**, *Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media*, **91 FR 44976–45131** (156 pages).

(b) Published **July 17, 2026**; effective **September 15, 2026**.

(c) **DHS Docket No. ICEB-2025-0001; RIN 1653-AA95** (DHS/ICE; classified as a major rule subject to congressional review).

(d) It finalizes the NPRM at **FR Doc. 2025-16554, 90 FR 42070 (Aug. 28, 2025)** (same docket and RIN).

(e) As of Nov. 14, 2026 **nothing has changed the effective date**: a docket search (ICEB-2025-0001) returns only the final rule, and no Federal Register notice under the rule's own DATES clause has appeared. Two things could still bear on it: (i) the DATES clause states that if the effective date is changed at the conclusion of congressional review (Congressional Review Act), DHS 'will publish a document in the Federal Register to establish the actual effective date or to terminate the rule' (91 FR 44976-44977; see also 5 U.S.C. 801-808 discussion at 91 FR 45119); and (ii) the rule is expressly **severable** (8 CFR 214.1(m)(4), 214.2(f)(20), 214.2(i)(8), 214.2(j)(6)), so a partial vacatur would not necessarily take down the F-1 fixed-admission provisions. Separately, DHS may delay or suspend only the change-of-objective/transfer provisions (f)(5)(ii)(A)-(C) until **Sept. 14, 2028** by Federal Register notice (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E)) - that affects implementation of specific paragraphs, not the effective date of the rule.

Q2.answer:
(a) **July 14, 2027.** Provision: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (transition rule for aliens in D/S who were maintaining status on Sept. 15, 2026). Arithmetic: start = I-20 program end date **May 15, 2027** (she has no EAD, so the EAD alternative is not 'later'); add the F-1 departure period of **60 days** = **July 14, 2027** (May 16-31 = 16 days; June 30 days = 46; July 14 = 60). This is below the rule's ceiling (Sept. 15, 2026 + 4 years = Sept. 15, 2030; + 60 days = Nov. 14, 2030).

(b) **F-1: November 14, 2030. J-1: October 15, 2030.** 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1): 4 years from Sept. 15, 2026 = Sept. 15, 2030, plus 60 days (F) = Nov. 14, 2030; plus 30 days (J) = Oct. 15, 2030 (the rule states both dates expressly).

(c) **Yes, as far as timing goes.** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G) requires her to begin classes 'within 5 months of transferring out of the current school or within 5 months of the program completion date on his or her current Form I-20, whichever is earlier.' Deadline: May 15, 2027 + 5 months = **October 15, 2027**; her Aug. 24, 2027 start is inside that window. She also satisfies the other transfer conditions on the stated assumptions: maintaining status ((f)(8)(i)(A)); has completed a degree program ((f)(8)(i)(B)(2)); is not 'currently in a graduate level program' ((f)(8)(i)(C)); has completed her first academic year at the school that issued her I-20 ((f)(8)(i)(D), Aug. 2023-Aug. 2024); and moving from bachelor's to master's is progression to a higher level, which the rule treats as maintaining status ((f)(5)(ii)(B)) and does not bar under the same-or-lower-level prohibition ((f)(5)(ii)(C)).

(d) **Yes - she must file Form I-539 with USCIS to extend her stay for the master's program** (assuming she stays in the United States; the transfer itself does not give her a new period of stay). Supporting provisions: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (transition aliens who 'would like to start a new program of study ... must apply for an extension of stay with USCIS in accordance with paragraph (c)(2)'); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iv) (if the new program 'will not be completed within the authorized period of stay,' the student must apply for EOS with a valid, endorsed I-20); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)-(iii) (eligibility, DSO-endorsed I-20, form, fee, biometrics, timely filing); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(D) (change of educational objective: EOS required); 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) (general EOS filing requirement); 8 CFR 214.1(c)(3)(v) (D/S aliens covered by (m) are not exempt from filing). The OPT-only I-539 exemption in 214.1(m)(1)(i) does not apply to a new degree program.

(e) **She files only Form I-765 (no I-539) for that OPT period**, provided she files before her period of admission expires (including the 60-day departure period) and **on or before March 18, 2027** - 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i). Her March 1, 2027 filing qualifies. If approved as requested, she may remain until the EAD end date (June 13, 2028) **plus 60 days = August 12, 2028** (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i): 'until the expiration date of the Employment Authorization Document, plus 60 days'; June 14-30 = 17 days, July 31 = 48, Aug. 12 = 60). Note her requested OPT start date (June 14, 2027) is exactly 30 days after her program end date, consistent with 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(D) as amended (60 replaced by 30).
